medium.en.asr: Austria, England and the Dutch backed a rival for Spain's crown, France backed Madrid's king. That summer their fleet sailed into the Bay of Gibraltar. Its commanders, Admiral George Rook and Prince George of Hesse -Darmstadt, fought for the rival claimant, Charles III. This plan, printed in 1705, shows the prize, a walled town that historians on both sides would call the key of the Mediterranean. Inside, Governor D. A. Gaudet Salih Nas had barely a hundred soldiers by a Spanish count. He refused to surrender. The fleet answered with some 15 ,000 rounds by British and Spanish accounts alike. On the 4th of August 1704, by the new calendar, Gibraltar surrendered. British accounts put the defenders at up to 500 counting armed townsmen. Townspeople could stay if they swore loyalty to Charles III. By a British account, almost all left. By a Spanish one, the largest group settled a league northeast at San Roque. In 1713, the Treaty of Utrecht gave it to the British crown forever, but without any territorial jurisdiction and without any open communication by land. If Britain ever gave it up, Spain would have first refusal. The treaty names the town, castle and port, not the sandy isthmus to the north. Spain says the isthmus was never ceded. Britain said in 2015 that Gibraltar includes it. Within weeks, Spain and France besieged it into 1705. Spain tried again in 1727. Neither siege took it. So in 1730, Philip V ordered a stone line across the isthmus, out of gun range, to cut Gibraltar off by land. The town behind it is still called La Linaire, the line.

medium.en.asr: Half a century later came a different question. Can you starve a rock? On the 21st of June 1779, Madrid cut Gibraltar off from Spain. Spain had joined France in its war with Britain. By October, British intelligence put the Spanish army facing the rock at up to 14 ,000. At sea from mid -July, a Spanish squadron sealed the port. Based at Alhaciras, its boats were there to cut off the food reaching the rock from Africa. By January 1780, thistles, dandelions and wild leeks were daily food for many. An egg cost sixpence. The governor, General Elliott, could hold the walls. The food had to come by sea. To break the blockade, Britain sent three relief fleets. 1780, 1781, 1782. Scurvy spread until a Danish ship of lemons was brought in, Garrison Diaries record. On the 12th of April 1781, the second relief convoy dropped anchor and Spain's batteries opened fire on the town. The townspeople fled south. Two days later, soldiers broke into the merchant's stores. A British officer blamed resentment and intoxication. By British tallies, the two sides fired over 460 ,000 rounds. By September 1782, the garrison counted about seven and a half thousand men. That summer, they had been digging through the north face. By early July, Sergeant Ince's 13 men had cut about 82 feet of solid rock. In July, they blasted a hole for air. A Spanish historian wrote it was big enough for a cannon. The garrison turned to heat. Cannonballs heated red hot. So that whatever they hit caught fire. On the 8th of September, they used them in earnest against the Spanish works. Four days later, the French and Spanish fleets gathered in the bay. 47 ships of the line by the British count, 50 by the Spanish. The Duc du Crillon led the siege. Their answer to red hot shot, 10 floating batteries designed by the French engineer Darcon. A French account says he'd asked to test them against red hot shot first. It was refused. The 13th of September 1782. That morning, the batteries moved into position under the garrison's fire. At 10 .25 by the Spanish account, the attacker's guns, some 400, opened fire together. By the next afternoon, all 10 batteries were lost. Over 2 ,000 attackers were lost by a British estimate that includes prisoners, and by a Spanish one. The British rescued 357. The blockade never forced a surrender. In February 1783, word came of a preliminary peace. And on the 5th, the last shot was fired. Spanish historian Montair O put losses near 2 ,000 defenders, and from all causes, 6 ,000 besiegers. The garrison's records count fewer dead, at least 869. Gibraltar stayed British.

medium.en.asr: Which leaves a question the treaty never answered. Where does the rock end? Between the walls and the Spanish line lay a strip of sand, the neutral ground. Around 1810, with Napoleon's armies heading for the strait, Spain and Britain were allies. With Spain's consent, the British blew up the Spanish forts. After that, the edge kept moving. A Spanish historian describes Britain advancing into the neutral zone, step by step. On the Spanish side, a town grew up behind the old line. In 1870 it became La Linaire de la Concepción. Remember this street in La Linaire, we'll come back to it. This was the gap between them, a strip of neutral ground between two towns. In 1908, Britain told Spain, as an act of courtesy, that it would fence the edge of the neutral ground. The fence went up in 1909. Spain does not recognise it as a border. Behind the fence, a garrison camp, gardens, rifle ranges, a race course. And from 1934, a grass airstrip was built there. Subscribe if you'd like the next place in this series.

medium.en.asr: Why build an airfield on disputed ground? In March 1939, Spain protested that the works stood on a usurped portion of its territory. That November, Spain's foreign minister called the strip a fête -à -com -pli, like the rock itself, while insisting its use breached Spanish territory. Late in 1939, Britain began a hard runway. In 1941, it was laid across the only road to Spain. Then, Britain pushed it out into the bay, with stone blasted from the north face and rubble from new tunnels. Inside the rock, those tunnels held a road about a mile long, a hospital and a power station dug by British and Canadian tunnellers. Gibraltar counts about 55 kilometres of tunnels from every era, more than its roads above ground. This 1943 US Army map shows the townhouse by house and the runway reaching into the bay. May 1940. Gibraltar sends its women and children away. June, Spain turns non -belligerent and occupies Tangier. By 1942, the invasion of North Africa is run from inside the rock. For the rest of the war, a Spanish scholar found Spain protested what it called breaches of Spanish waters. No complaint over the airstrip is on record. On the night of the 7th of November 1942, by Gibraltar's official record, at least 650 aircraft lined the runway. The invasion fleets from Britain and the United States came through the strait.
